intro: An FDE's code only matters if the customer understands it, trusts it and decides to use it, and that depends on communication as much as engineering. This lesson covers the communication that fills an FDE's week: demos that land, weekly status updates that surface risk early, short design documents that get decisions made, managing expectations and saying no without damaging the relationship, and escalating problems before they become crises.
objectives: Structure and run a demo that ends in a decision
Write a weekly status update that makes risks and asks impossible to miss
Use short design documents to get technical decisions agreed
Manage expectations and decline requests with clear trade-offs
Escalate early, with evidence and options, to the right person

sections.heading: Demos that end in a decision

blocks.text: A demo is not a feature tour. It is a short story with a purpose: remind the audience of the problem, show the software solving it on their real data, show the evidence that it works, and ask for something. Keep it to the minimum that makes the point, usually fifteen to twenty minutes plus discussion.

items: **Problem (1-2 minutes):** the pain in their words and numbers, from discovery.
**Live walkthrough (8-10 minutes):** one realistic case end to end, using a real (approved) example, ideally driven by a user rather than by you.
**Evidence (3-5 minutes):** metric versus baseline, evaluation results, user quotes.
**Limits and risks (2 minutes):** what it does not do yet, honestly.
**Ask (1 minute):** the decision or help you need, with a date.

blocks.text: Rehearse with the exact data and environment, have a recorded backup in case the network or a dependency fails, and never demo something you have not run that morning. A demo that fails on stage costs more trust than one that is modest.

Send a written update every week, to the same people, in the same format. Its main job is not to report activity but to make **risks** and **asks** visible early, while they are still cheap to fix. Lead with an honest overall status.

blocks.caption: A status update that takes two minutes to read
blocks.code:
Subject: Claims assistant pilot - week 3 status: AMBER

Summary: Working version live for 5 of 12 handlers; accuracy on track;
security review not yet scheduled, which puts the week-5 rollout at risk.

Done this week
- Clause lookup working on 1,800 motor policies; 96% accurate on 120 reviewed cases
- 5 handlers using it daily; median lookup time 40s (baseline 6 min)

Next week
- Onboard remaining 7 handlers; expand evaluation set to 200 cases

Risks
- Security review unscheduled (owner: InfoSec). If not booked by Fri, rollout slips 1+ week.

Asks
- Sponsor: please help us book the security review this week.
- Team lead: 2 hours of reviewer time on Tuesday.

items: Status colours mean something: green on track, amber at risk with a plan, red will miss without a decision. Do not stay green until the week before failure.
Every risk has an owner and a consequence; every ask has a person and a date.
Use numbers, not adjectives: "96% on 120 cases" rather than "accuracy is good".

blocks.text: When a technical choice affects the customer (where data is processed, how you integrate with their system, what they will have to operate), write a one-to-two-page design note rather than deciding in a meeting. Written options get better feedback, include people who could not attend, and leave a record of why a decision was made.

items: **Context**: the problem and constraints in a few sentences.
**Options**: two or three, each with benefits, costs, risks and what the customer must do.
Afterwards, record the decision at the top and keep the document with the project.

blocks.text: Customers excited by a working prototype will ask for more: another use case, another data source, a mobile app. Saying yes to everything wrecks the pilot; saying no flatly damages the relationship. Make trade-offs visible instead: "We can add home policies; it would push the decision meeting by two weeks, or we could swap out the export feature. Which do you prefer?" The sponsor decides, with the consequences in view.

Set expectations about AI behaviour early and concretely. Show examples of mistakes the system makes and how they are caught, explain what the evaluation measures and what it does not, and avoid language that implies certainty. Customers forgive known limitations; they do not forgive surprises.
Never promise dates or features on behalf of your product team in a customer meeting. Say you will find out, then follow up in writing.

Escalation is not failure; late escalation is. Escalate when a blocker threatens a milestone and you cannot remove it yourself within a few days: access that is not arriving, a stakeholder who has gone silent, a technical limitation in your product, a scope dispute.

items: State the problem and its impact on the plan in one or two sentences.
Show what you have already tried.
Offer options, each with its consequence, and your recommendation.
Name the decision or help you need and the date it is needed by.
Send it to the person who can actually decide, and keep your customer champion informed so it is never a surprise to them.

blocks.text: Escalate inside your own company too: product gaps, bugs blocking a customer, or a deal at risk. Your account team, product managers and engineering leads can only help with problems they know about.

practice.title: Communication drills
steps: Script a 15-minute demo of any project you have built using the five-part structure, then record yourself delivering it.
Write a week-3 status update for an imaginary pilot that is AMBER, with two risks and two asks with owners and dates.
Write a one-page design note comparing two ways to integrate with a customer system, ending with a decision request.
Write a reply to a sponsor asking for a big new feature mid-pilot that offers two trade-off options.
Write an escalation message about data access that is two weeks late, following the five steps.
Ask a friend outside tech to read the status update and tell you what the risks are; rewrite until they can.

focus: Demo = problem, live real case, evidence, limits, ask.
Weekly status in a fixed format; risks and asks are the point.
Write design notes with options for decisions that affect the customer.
Say no with trade-offs and let the sponsor choose.
Escalate early with evidence, options and a date.

items.desc: Real data, ideally a user driving
Honest gaps, decision needed by date

items.syntax: decision needed by DATE, to DECIDER

pitfalls: Feature-tour demos with no problem statement and no ask.
Green status until the week before a missed deadline.
Deciding customer-affecting architecture verbally with no record.
Promising product features or dates you do not control.
Escalating only after a milestone has already been missed.

quiz.q: What should a pilot demo end with?
options: A clear ask for a decision or help, with a date
A list of every feature that was built
A promise of what the next release will contain
Questions about the customer's budget
quiz.explain: Demos exist to move the engagement forward; ending with a specific ask turns attention into a decision.

quiz.q: The security review is unscheduled and threatens next month's rollout. How should this week's status look?
options: AMBER, with the risk, its owner, the consequence and an ask
GREEN, because engineering work is on track
RED, with no explanation, to get attention
No mention until the review is booked
quiz.explain: Amber with a named risk and a specific ask surfaces the problem while it is still cheap to fix.

quiz.q: A sponsor asks for a large new feature mid-pilot. What is the best response?
options: Offer options with their effect on timeline or scope and let them choose
Accept it and absorb the extra work quietly
Decline because it is not in the SOW
Promise it for the next product release
quiz.explain: Visible trade-offs keep you helpful while protecting the pilot; the sponsor decides knowing the cost.

quiz.q: When should you escalate a blocked data-access request?
options: When it threatens a milestone and you cannot unblock it within days
Only after the milestone has been missed
Never, because escalation damages relationships
Only if the customer asks you to
quiz.explain: Early escalation with evidence and options gives decision makers time to act; late escalation only explains a failure.

quiz.q: Why write a short design note instead of deciding an integration approach in a meeting?
options: It gathers better feedback and records why the decision was made
Meetings are not allowed at customer sites
Design notes replace the need for code reviews
It delays the decision, which reduces risk
quiz.explain: Written options include absent stakeholders, improve the decision and leave a record when people later ask why.
